title: WayfinderAI
tagline: AI-powered indoor navigation — no GPS, just vision
description: Two independent works under the same project — not yet integrated, but sharing the same goal: indoor navigation without GPS, beacons, or hardware.

parts.label: Part 1 — VLM Floorplan Pipeline (NaviGrid)
parts.summary: Built a fully automated 3-phase data pipeline to generate 4,248 VLM training pairs from 100 CubiCasa5K floor plans — zero manual annotation — then fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-8B via LoRA + GRPO to convert raw floor plan images into structured navigation graphs.
bullets: Phase 1: SVG parsing via ElementTree extracts room nodes (kitchen, hallway, bathroom, stairs) with bounding boxes and center coordinates

Phase 2: Algorithmic edge inference using proximity thresholds + corridor filtering + entrance-rooted BFS; direction-tagged ST/TL/TR/SA via atan2 geometry; LLaMA 3.2 generates plain English directions
Phase 3: 5-type QA pair generation (treemap, route, location-nav, spatial, multi-turn) → 4,248 pairs (3,824 train / 424 val) for Qwen3-VL fine-tuning
Baseline evaluation: direction similarity 0.746, plain English score 0.950, graph connectivity 100% — 8/15 inference successes (OOM crashes on remaining)
GRPO reward-based fine-tuning produced valid navigation graph JSON more reliably than supervised fine-tuning alone

parts.label: Part 2 — Kroger Grocery Navigation App
parts.summary: Sequential 5-agent pipeline guides users through Kroger stores — from natural language shopping input to real-time shelf-position guidance — using only the Kroger Developer API. No beacons, no GPS. Won 1st Place at Hack@URI AI Track (30+ teams).
bullets: Agent 0: Ollama llama3.2 converts recipes or meal ideas → verified Kroger shopping list with live price checks
Agent 1: Kroger API → NetworkX graph (34 aisles, 110+ connections) in <0.15s
Agent 2: Dual routing — Dijkstra in-order vs nearest-neighbor greedy; always picks 10-30% shorter path with real geometry-based turn directions
Agent 3: EasyOCR reads physical aisle signs (A1–A42) every 5th frame to confirm real-world location; Claude Vision fallback on low-confidence reads
Agent 4: YOLO-World open-vocabulary detection (no fine-tuning); 3-frame confirmation window; reports 9-region shelf position from bounding box centroid
FastAPI backend + React 18 frontend with interactive SVG store map and voice readout per direction

title: Apex AI
tagline: Vision-only AI race engineer — no sensors, just video
description: AI race engineer that watches your onboard karting or motorcycle lap and delivers structured coaching — timestamped mistakes, best moments, performance scores, and lap time loss estimates. Built in two separate versions.
inspiration: I got the initial idea at the Vision Hackathon. Most teams were focused on executing existing ideas and hoping their implementation would stand out — I took a different approach and worked on something I was genuinely passionate about: Formula 1. I've always been drawn to finding ways to minimize the cost of sensors and heavy data processing in motorsport. That's where Apex/PitLane AI came from — upload an onboard lap video and get back structured race engineering insights. What race engineers do by analyzing sensor telemetry, this does from video alone.

parts.label: V1 — PitLane AI (Twelve Labs)
parts.summary: Powered by two Twelve Labs models — Pegasus for whole-video semantic analysis and Marengo for video search. Won the Twelve Labs Computer Vision Hackathon at Northeastern University.
bullets: Pegasus watches the full lap and finds errors across 4 categories: Racing Line, Braking, Throttle & Traction, Car Control
Find Best Moments across 6 categories — smooth apex, clean acceleration, perfect racing line, and more
Ask free-form questions: 'Where am I losing the most time?' — returns verdict + timestamped moments
Coaching report: performance scores (1–10), sector breakdown, lap time loss in tenths of seconds, top 3 fixes
Two surfaces: FiftyOne plugin (run operators on video dataset) + React web app

parts.label: V2 — Apex AI (Fully Local)
parts.futurePlans: Experiment further with modularity — local models feel like the right direction here. The pipeline is computationally heavy, and rather than building a general-purpose system, a more expert-driven approach would be stronger: purpose-built pipelines that only activate models relevant to the specific application, and deliver results shaped around what that sport or discipline actually demands.
parts.summary: I wanted to avoid relying on paid API models and instead explore how far a fully local, modular pipeline could go — breaking the task into small pieces each handled by a lightweight local model. Supports karting, biking, and cycling from a single onboard video.
bullets: Stage 1: CV events loader — YOLOv8n + Farneback optical flow extracts braking, racing line, and speed delta events with severity scores
Stage 2: Florence-2-base (232M params, CPU) triages each keyframe — vehicle_visible, in_corner, obstacle_ahead via <CAPTION> + <OD> tasks
Stage 3: Conditional llava reasoning via Ollama — only fires on significant events or obstacle frames, skips the rest
Stage 4: Parallel llama3.2 coaching note writer — asyncio + ThreadPoolExecutor (4 workers) generates per-event coaching notes concurrently
Stage 5: llama3.2 session aggregator synthesises all notes into a final structured coaching report
CV-only fallback mode when Ollama is unavailable — no hard API dependency

challenges: V1: Twelve Labs returns rich but unstructured observations — getting Groq LLaMA to extract valid JSON performance scores without hallucinating required careful prompt engineering and retry logic. V2: Florence-2's <OD> task on CPU is ~1–3s per frame — running it on every frame would take hours. The fix was a two-gate system: only triage keyframes flagged by the CV events loader, then only invoke llava on frames that pass Florence-2's severity threshold.
learnings: The API approach (V1) is undeniably more reliable — Twelve Labs Pegasus produces richer, more accurate coaching than anything a local pipeline can match today. But the modular local approach (V2) showed that dividing the problem into small focused tasks — each handled by the right lightweight model — gets you surprisingly far without spending a dollar. The two versions are not competing; they represent two different constraints, and both are worth knowing.

title: Edge AI Multisensor System
tagline: Distributed edge intelligence for building automation with multi-sensor pipelines
description: A multi-hub edge AI system that runs 5 parallel edge hub threads — each monitoring a building zone via real BMS sensor data (VAVs, RTUs) — and a central coordinator that escalates anomalies. All AI runs locally via Ollama. No cloud, no latency, no data leaving the building.
longDescription: Each edge hub polls live VAV (variable air volume) and RTU (rooftop unit) sensor readings, computes divergence scores against setpoints, and classifies anomalies as moderate or critical using an active inference framework. Critical events are escalated to a CVC (central validation coordinator) running llama3.2 locally. The system supports 8 named fault scenarios — from single zone overheat to a full multi-hub crisis — and sends alerts via Telegram to engineers and operators.
highlights: 5 parallel edge hub threads, each monitoring a dedicated building zone independently
Real BMS data: 26 VAVs + 4 RTUs across 5 zones — real sensor readings, not mocked
Active inference anomaly detection — divergence score triggers moderate/critical classification
Ollama llama3.2 runs entirely locally — no cloud API calls, no data leaves the building
8 named fault scenarios: zone overheat, sensor loss, power surge, RTU fault, multi-hub crisis
Telegram alerting to separate engineer and operator channels on critical events
challenges: Designing a two-level model hierarchy (hub LLM + CVC LLM) where each hub acts independently but the coordinator synthesises across all zones required careful message passing and timeout handling — if a hub is slow, the CVC can't block waiting for it.
learnings: Edge AI for physical infrastructure is fundamentally different from cloud AI — latency, reliability, and data residency constraints dominate design decisions more than raw accuracy. Running llama3.2 locally was non-negotiable for a real building deployment.

title: Intelligent Follow-Me Robot
tagline: Vision + IMU person-following robot — Android phone as the only sensor
description: A person-following robot that uses an Android phone as its only sensor — streaming live video and IMU data over WiFi to a Flask server running the full vision pipeline. The server sends BLE motor commands to an Elegoo UNO R4 WiFi robot in real time, with no GPU required.
longDescription: The pipeline runs frame-by-frame entirely on CPU. Each frame goes through adaptive YOLO26n detection, 3-zone ReID enrollment (head / upper / lower body MobileNetV2 embeddings + HSV colour histograms + gait signature), KCF tracking between YOLO frames, and Kalman smoothing — before a 3-stage safety check (Step 32 obstacle heuristics → local reflex layer → safety governor) approves the BLE command. IMU data gates ReID on shaky frames and suspends tracker re-init during fast turns. When the target is lost, gyro integration drives directional search sweeps until re-acquisition.
highlights: Android phone as the only sensor — IP Webcam MJPEG stream + /sensors.json IMU at ~50Hz
3-zone ReID: MobileNetV2 embeddings (head/upper/lower) + HSV colour histograms + gait (ankle oscillation)
Adaptive YOLO interval — motion-gated so YOLO only runs when needed; KCF handles in-between frames
Hard YOLO veto rule: zero-person detection immediately overrides tracker output (prevents wall drift)
3-stage safety pipeline: Step 32 heuristics → local reflex layer → safety governor
Lost-person recovery using gyro-integrated search sweeps with 15° direction flips
challenges: The KCF tracker drifts onto walls when the target is lost — fixed with a hard YOLO veto rule: if YOLO runs and finds zero people, the tracker output is discarded entirely, no exceptions. On the hardware side, the stock Elegoo firmware required a reset after every BLE disconnect — a custom Arduino sketch fixes this by restarting BLE advertising automatically on disconnect.
learnings: The IMU isn't tracking the person — it's tracking the robot. Using accelerometer shake to skip ReID on blurry frames and gyro yaw to gate tracker re-init during fast turns made the system dramatically more robust without adding any extra sensors. The right question wasn't 'how do I track the person better' but 'how do I know when not to trust the tracker at all'.

title: Star Tracker CNN
tagline: Benchmarking U-Net variants for star detection in CubeSat star trackers
description: Research project benchmarking three U-Net architectures for star detection and sub-pixel centroid localisation on real DSS2 sky images — targeting CubeSat constraints where model size, inference time, and accuracy all matter equally.
longDescription: Part of the Northeastern Satellite Lab CubeSat Star Tracker project. Trained and evaluated UNet (482K params), MobileUNet (255K params), and ELUNet (60K params, based on arXiv:2404.19108) on 250 real 256×256 sky images from NASA SkyView's DSS2 Red Survey. Ground truth segmentation maps were generated by Gaussian blur → brightness thresholding → connected component size filtering. ELUNet outputs a dual-channel head — segmentation + distance map regression — enabling trilateration-based sub-pixel centroiding without any post-processing. INT8 quantization (post-training + LSQ fine-tuning) compresses ELUNet from 232 KB to 60 KB with less than 0.003 F1 loss, making it the strongest candidate for deployment on a Raspberry Pi.
challenges: MobileUNet — despite having fewer parameters than UNet — was the slowest model at inference. The inverted residual blocks with depthwise separable convolutions that make MobileNet efficient on classification don't translate well to dense segmentation at 256×256 resolution. ELUNet's single-conv blocks with batch norm proved both faster and more quantization-friendly than MobileUNet's expanded residuals.
learnings: The metric that matters for satellite hardware isn't F1 alone — it's F1 per millisecond per kilobyte. ELUNet's aggressive channel reduction (base_ch=8 vs 16 for UNet) and single-conv blocks make it quantization-friendly: INT8 drops F1 by only 0.003 while cutting model size 3.86×. The dual output head — predicting segmentation and distance maps simultaneously — also gave sub-pixel centroid accuracy through trilateration without adding any post-processing overhead.
